newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-COURT HEARS OF GROBBELAAR ANGUISH OVER FAILURE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-COURT HEARS OF GROBBELAAR ANGUISH OVER FAILURE.

text.p: Britain was given a glimpse of the thought processes of English soccer's most eccentric goalkeeper on Wednesday as a court was treated to the greatest saves of Bruce Grobbelaar on video tape.

Grobbelaar, the league game's most successful keeper, is accused of fixing matches for money when he was the last line of defence for one of England's great post-war sides, Liverpool. He denies the charges.

The jury in the most sensational match-fixing case here in more than 30 years must consider whether a goalkeeper, whose prowess depends on reflexes, positioning and speed, can decide in a millisecond to deliberately miss a shot, give away a goal -- but not make it look deliberate.
Secret recordings reveal Grobbelaar was both angry and anguished about his failure to rig games for an Asian betting syndicate, the court in Winchester, southern England, heard.
The tapes form the backbone to the match-rigging charges against Grobbelaar, a brilliant keeper known as the "clown prince of English soccer", and three other defendants.

The keeper picked up 40,000 pounds ($66,930) after Liverpool lost 3-0 to Newcastle in November 1993 but blew his chance of a huge reward in January 1994 when, despite his best (or worst) efforts Liverpool drew 3-3 with Manchester United, the prosecution alleges.
"If the ball doesn't play, it doesn't play. In the Manchester United game, do you know how much money I lost? 125,000 pounds in cash," he said in the recordings, which were peppered with expletives.

"In the second half I made two blinding saves. I dived the wrong way and went `Phew' and the ball hit my hand," said Grobbelaar, who according to the prosecution decided to tamper with games because he was unhappy with his Liverpool wages.
Video footage of two incidents during the game played in court showed the keeper using his hands to deflect fierce shots from Ryan Giggs and Roy Keane past the post.
He took bigger risks with an attempt to engineer Liverpool's defeat against Norwich in February 1994, but to the syndicate's anger, it ended in a 2-2 draw, the prosecution said.

According to chief prosecution witness Chris Vincent, a former business partner of Grobbelaar, the goalkeeper sneaked out of the team hotel at Norwich late the night before the game and drove to London to pick up cash from the syndicate.
Grobbelaar picked up 500 pounds from fellow defendant and alleged syndicate middleman Heng Suan Lim, who he called the Short Man, it was alleged.
According to the tapes Grobbelaar blamed the drawn result on an instinctive save he made with his legs from Norwich player Jeremy Goss.
"I'm my own worst enemy in that I don't like to lose. So it's instinct," the court heard him saying.

In July 1994 he flew to Malaysia, ostensibly for a friendly tournament, but in reality to show the syndicate what he was made of, the court heard. The tapes show he was surprised when the betting group promptly rigged the tournament to make money.
"The Short Man's boss is big in Malaysia. That's it -- finish," he said, making a motion as if to slit his throat. "It's frightening. There must be so much money out there."

Grobbelaar complained that the syndicate told him to fix matches without checking first whether it could easily be done, as was the case with Southampton's away game to perennial strugglers Coventry in late September 1994.

"So two minutes into the game I push the ball into the back of the net. And then we steamrollered them," said the keeper. Southampton eventually won 3-1 and the risks he was taking evidently started to weigh more on him.
"If I get caught, I'm out. Then my family life is gone and they'll be looked at as well. My wife doesn't know anything. If it gets out she's going to ask questions," he said on the tape.
In November 1994, the Sun newspaper printed the allegations which triggered the present court case. ($1=.5976 Pound)
